claims.text: Controlled segregation of Al or Ti during processing induces a continuous nanoscale oxide/nitride precipitate network along grain or phase boundaries in AlCoCrFeNi-based HEAs.
The boundary precipitate network lowers alloy density by limiting clustering or redistribution of heavy elements.
The proposed precipitate network increases mechanical strength through precipitation strengthening.
The proposed precipitate network acts as a self-healing barrier against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Increasing Al or Ti content and controlling the cooling rate will promote elemental segregation and formation of the proposed continuous precipitate network.
A continuous nanoscale oxide/nitride network is the structural mediator linking processing to the targeted properties.
The passivating precipitate network improves both corrosion resistance and oxidation resistance.
The segregated alloy will have lower density than the homogenized AlCoCrFeNi-based baseline.
The segregated alloy will have greater mechanical strength than the homogenized baseline.
The segregated alloy will have better corrosion resistance than the homogenized baseline.
The segregated alloy will have better high-temperature oxidation resistance than the homogenized baseline.
Excessive elemental segregation or grain-boundary precipitation can produce brittle phases and degrade mechanical integrity.
Excessive segregation will make the protective precipitate network discontinuous or overly coarsened.
Excessive light-element content can destabilize the alloy phase structure.
Rapid cooling can be used to promote controlled elemental segregation in the experimental alloy.
Exposure to 3.5 wt% NaCl and high-temperature oxidizing atmospheres provides a relevant simulation of aerospace and rail service environments.
Failure to observe the proposed network, or failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in all targeted properties, is designated as falsification of the hypothesis.
